author: CC
prose: THE BEAT COSTS TEN SECONDS AGAINST A ONE-SECOND CADENCE, AND 84% OF IT IS THREE SHIMS RE-DERIVING THE WHOLE CORPUS EVERY BEAT. CADENCE_S = 1.0 is Akien's ruling (2026-07-30) and __main__.py honours it exactly — beat(), then sleep(1.0). The sleep is not the problem; the beat is. Measured today under an isolated instance root so the instrument did not seed the tree it reads: a warm beat is 8.7-9.3s at ~76% of a core, sustained, forever. Per-shim, timing each on_pulse individually over two rounds: base 3.1-3.5s (33%), inference_domain 2.7-4.1s (29%), build_inspector 2.1-3.2s (22%) — 84% between three of twenty-two shims, while ELEVEN shims together cost 0.05s. cProfile on one beat names the mechanism rather than the culprit: 1,645 calls to builtins.compile (3.1s), 1.6 MILLION ast.walk steps (8.2s cumulative), 37,722 json.raw_decode calls (2.6s), and 32 psycopg2 round trips. The named hot leaves are address_rule.spellings_in (5.5s cumulative over 576 calls), import_sieve.imports_in (3.1s over 332 calls), and deviceness._class_census (2.2s, AST-parsing the corpus twice). The shape of the defect is one sentence: SEVERAL PROBES EACH INDEPENDENTLY WALK THE SAME 331 FILES ON EVERY BEAT, to answer questions whose answers only change when a file changes. That is Law 1's defect on a one-second clock — the settled re-derived, 8.6 million times a day — and the standing aim of an ever-shrinking compute footprint says the trigger should be the file changing, not the clock ticking. Cheapest honest fix is a corpus index built once and invalidated by mtime, shared by every probe that asks; the Cairn-native fix is that a probe whose question is about the corpus subscribes to the corpus changing.
